planting.note: Set the large bulbs 6-8 inches deep in fall so roots establish before the ground freezes.

directions: Ambassador produces one of the tallest and largest flower spheres of the giant onion group, with densely packed violet-purple globes reaching up to eight inches across on sturdy four-foot stems. Give it full sun and sharply drained soil, since standing winter moisture rots the bulbs. It bridges the bloom gap between earlier Globemaster and later A. giganteum, extending the ornamental onion season by several weeks. Leave the seed heads standing after bloom for continued garden interest and easy naturalizing.

planting.note: Plant bulbs deeply in fall in a spot with excellent drainage to prevent rot over winter.

directions: This giant hybrid onion bears some of the largest flower heads in cultivation, with lavender-purple globes eight to ten inches wide atop stout three- to four-foot stems. Plant where heavy clay is amended or use raised beds, since the bulbs are prone to rot in wet winter soil. The bold strappy foliage forms an attractive low rosette that fades as the flower stalk rises, so pair with later-emerging perennials to mask it. Deadheading is unnecessary since the dried seed heads remain ornamental for weeks.

planting.note: Install bulbs in fall in groups of ten or more for a dramatic massed display the following spring.

directions: His Excellency is a robust, self-naturalizing giant onion that produces violet-blue globes roughly five inches across on stems that can top five feet. It tolerates a wide range of soils from sandy to gritty loam as long as drainage is good, and once established it returns and multiplies for years with minimal care. Grow it toward the back of a border where its height provides vertical structure among lower perennials. It is highly attractive to bees and other pollinators while remaining reliably deer- and rabbit-resistant.

planting.note: Plant in fall alongside late tulips and daffodils, since this cultivar flowers earlier than most giant alliums.

directions: Early Emperor blooms noticeably earlier than typical giganteum-type alliums, opening its dense purple-violet globes alongside late tulips and camas. It holds an RHS Award of Garden Merit for its reliable performance and garden-worthy habit. Grow in full sun with sharp drainage, and let the broad basal leaves die back naturally after bloom rather than braiding or removing them early. Because it flowers early in the allium succession, it extends the ornamental onion display when paired with later-blooming giants like Globemaster or Ambassador.

planting.note: Tuck bulbs into a sunny, gritty spot near the border edge where the broad foliage can be appreciated.

directions: This dwarf Turkestan onion cultivar is grown as much for its broad, blue-green, strap-shaped leaves as for its creamy white globe flowers, which open in late spring atop short, sturdy stalks. It stays low and compact, making it well suited to rock gardens, containers, and the front of a dry perennial bed. Give it a spot that stays dry over summer once foliage fades, since the bulbs are prone to rot in constantly moist soil. It tolerates heat and drought once established and is exceptionally deer- and rodent-resistant.
